decks.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions — Part 1: Principal values and graphs
goals: Explain why a trigonometric function must be restricted before it can be inverted
State the domain and principal-value range of all six inverse trigonometric functions
Find principal values, including expressions such as the inverse sine of the sine of an angle
Find the domain of a function built from an inverse trigonometric function
Sketch the graphs of the inverse sine, cosine and tangent as reflections in y = x

slides.heading: Inverse Trigonometric Functions, Part 1
slides.body_md: Given a ratio, which angle? A calculator always answers with one particular angle.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: restrict a trigonometric function, take its principal-value branch, define the six inverse functions, find principal values, and draw their graphs as reflections.
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: A ramp rises one metre for every two metres along the ground. What is its angle? To answer, we must run the tangent function backwards. In this part you will learn how mathematicians choose one answer out of infinitely many, meet all six inverse trigonometric functions, and draw their graphs.

slides.heading: Why restrict first?
slides.body_md: $\sin x$ is many-one on $\mathbb{R}$, so it has no inverse. On $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ it is one-one and onto $[-1, 1]$.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals sin x from minus 6.6 to 6.6, a wave between minus 1 and 1. The piece from minus pi by 2 to pi by 2 is highlighted: it rises once from minus 1 to 1 and takes each value exactly once.
visual.caption: Many angles share a sine; the highlighted branch keeps exactly one of them.

slides.narration: The sine wave takes every value between minus one and one infinitely often, so it cannot be undone as it stands. Keep only the piece from minus pi by two to pi by two. On that piece the curve rises once and meets each value exactly once, so it has an inverse. That piece is called the principal-value branch.

slides.heading: The six principal-value branches
slides.body_md: Each inverse function returns angles only from its principal range.

visual.alt: Table of the six inverse trigonometric functions: sine and cosine inverses have domain minus 1 to 1, tangent and cotangent inverses have all reals, secant and cosecant inverses exclude the open interval minus 1 to 1; the principal ranges are listed beside each.
visual.caption: Learn this table: almost every principal-value question uses it.

slides.narration: Here are all six inverse functions. The inverse sine and inverse cosine accept numbers from minus one to one. The inverse tangent and inverse cotangent accept every real number. The inverse secant and inverse cosecant accept numbers outside the open interval from minus one to one. Notice that the cosine family uses ranges starting at zero.

slides.heading: The graph of the inverse sine
slides.body_md: $y = \sin^{-1} x$ rises from $\left(-1, -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ to $\left(1, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals the inverse sine of x for x from minus 1 to 1: it rises from the point minus 1, minus pi by 2 through the origin to the point 1, pi by 2, steepest at the two ends.
visual.caption: Domain $[-1, 1]$, range $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$; an odd, increasing function.

slides.narration: The inverse sine curve starts at minus one with height minus pi by two, passes through the origin and ends at one with height pi by two. It is increasing and it is odd: turning the input negative turns the output negative. The curve is steepest at its two ends.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: five principal values
slides.body_md: Find each value using the correct branch.

visual.alt: Worked example table of five principal values computed from the branches: inverse sine of minus one half is minus pi by 6, inverse cosine of root 3 by 2 is pi by 6, inverse tangent of minus 1 is minus pi by 4, inverse cotangent of minus 1 by root 3 is 2 pi by 3, inverse secant of root 2 is pi by 4.
visual.caption: Each value is checked numerically when the chapter is built.

slides.narration: For each value, first recall the branch, then find the one angle in it with the given ratio. The inverse sine of minus one half is minus pi by six. The inverse cotangent of a negative number must lie between pi by two and pi, so it is two pi by three. For the inverse secant, turn the secant into a cosine first.

slides.heading: Quick check: the inverse cotangent
slides.body_md: Choose the principal value of the inverse cotangent of a negative number.
slides.narration: Remember that the inverse cotangent never gives a negative angle. Its answers lie strictly between zero and pi.

slides.heading: The graph of the inverse cosine
slides.body_md: $y = \cos^{-1} x$ falls from $(-1, \pi)$ to $(1, 0)$.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals the inverse cosine of x: it falls from the point minus 1, pi through the point 0, pi by 2 to the point 1, 0 on the x-axis. It is a decreasing curve lying between heights 0 and pi.
visual.caption: Domain $[-1, 1]$, range $[0, \pi]$; a decreasing function.

slides.narration: The inverse cosine curve begins at the point minus one, pi, passes through zero, pi by two, and ends on the x axis at one. It is decreasing everywhere. Because its range is from zero to pi, it never gives a negative answer, which is why the inverse cosine of a negative number is an obtuse angle.

slides.heading: Inverse tangent and inverse cotangent
slides.body_md: Both are defined on all of $\mathbb{R}$; $\tan^{-1} x$ rises between $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $\cot^{-1} x$ falls between $\pi$ and $0$.

visual.alt: Graphs of the inverse tangent, rising between the horizontal asymptotes minus pi by 2 and pi by 2, and of the inverse cotangent, falling between pi and 0. They cross at the point 1, pi by 4, and the cotangent curve passes 0, pi by 2.
visual.caption: The two curves add up to $\frac{\pi}{2}$ at every $x$.

slides.narration: The inverse tangent accepts every real number and rises between two horizontal asymptotes at minus pi by two and pi by two. The inverse cotangent falls from pi towards zero. The two curves cross at the point one, pi by four, and at every input their heights add up to pi by two.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a domain from the argument
slides.body_md: Find the domain of $f(x) = \cos^{-1}\dfrac{2x - 1}{5}$.
bullets: The argument of the inverse cosine must lie in $[-1, 1]$

visual.alt: Worked example table for the domain of the inverse cosine of 2 x minus 1 over 5: the argument must lie between minus 1 and 1, which after multiplying by 5 and solving gives x from minus 2 to 3.
visual.caption: Domain $[-2, 3]$.

slides.narration: An inverse cosine only accepts numbers from minus one to one, so put the whole argument between minus one and one. Multiply through by five, add one and divide by two. The domain is the closed interval from minus two to three. Check an end point: at three the argument is exactly one.

slides.heading: Quick check: undoing a cosine
slides.body_md: An even function and a principal branch: which angle comes back?
slides.narration: Cosine does not change when the angle changes sign. Then ask whether the angle lies between zero and pi.

slides.heading: The inverse secant in two pieces
slides.body_md: $\sec^{-1} x$: domain $\mathbb{R} - (-1, 1)$, range $[0, \pi] - \left\{\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right\}$.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals the inverse secant of x in two pieces: for x at most minus 1 it rises from just above pi by 2 towards pi at x equals minus 1, and for x at least 1 it rises from 0 at x equals 1 towards pi by 2, passing 2, pi by 3. The height pi by 2 is never reached.
visual.caption: Domain $\mathbb{R} - (-1, 1)$; the line $y = \frac{\pi}{2}$ is an asymptote.

slides.narration: The inverse secant has two separate pieces, because the secant never takes values strictly between minus one and one. Both pieces rise. The height pi by two is never reached, since the secant of a right angle is undefined. To evaluate it, rewrite the secant as one over a cosine.

slides.heading: Inverse of a trigonometric value
slides.body_md: $\sin^{-1}(\sin\theta) = \theta$ only when $\theta \in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$; otherwise find the angle in the branch with the same sine.

visual.alt: Table of four angles, their sines and the inverse sine of each sine: only pi by 3 comes back unchanged; 5 pi by 6 returns pi by 6, 7 pi by 6 returns minus pi by 6, and minus 3 pi by 4 returns minus pi by 4.
visual.caption: The inverse sine always answers inside $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$.

slides.narration: Be careful with expressions like the inverse sine of the sine of an angle. They do not simply cancel. The answer must lie in the principal branch, so the inverse sine of the sine of seven pi by six is minus pi by six, not seven pi by six. The table shows four cases.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: inverse cosine of a cosine
slides.body_md: Find $\cos^{-1}\left(\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right)$.

visual.alt: Worked example table: the cosine of 5 pi by 3 equals the cosine of pi by 3, pi by 3 lies in the cosine branch from 0 to pi, so the inverse cosine of the cosine of 5 pi by 3 is pi by 3.
visual.caption: Find the angle in the branch with the same cosine.

slides.narration: The angle five pi by three is outside the cosine branch. Use the fact that cosine is unchanged when an angle is replaced by two pi minus the angle. That gives pi by three, which lies between zero and pi. So the inverse cosine of the cosine of five pi by three is pi by three.

slides.heading: Quick check: a decreasing inverse
slides.body_md: Which inverse function falls on its whole domain?
slides.narration: Picture each graph from left to right. Only one of them goes downhill all the way.

slides.heading: Graphs as reflections
slides.body_md: Reflect each principal branch in $y = x$ to get the inverse graph.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals sin x on its branch from minus pi by 2 to pi by 2, the inverse sine curve, and the mirror line y equals x. The point pi by 2, 1 on the sine curve reflects to the point 1, pi by 2 on the inverse curve; all three meet at the origin.
visual.caption: Each inverse graph is the mirror image of its branch in $y = x$.

slides.narration: Every inverse graph is the reflection of its branch in the line y equals x. The point pi by two, one on the sine branch becomes the point one, pi by two on the inverse sine curve. Use this to sketch any of the inverse graphs quickly in the examination.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false?
slides.body_md: Can an inverse sine ever equal two?
slides.narration: Compare two with the largest value the inverse sine can take, which is pi by two.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Restrict to a one-one branch, then invert
Learn the six domains and principal ranges
Graphs: reflect the branch in $y = x$

Table of six domains and ranges

visual.caption: Part 1 in one line.

slides.narration: To sum up this part. Each trigonometric function is first restricted to a branch where it is one-one. The inverse then returns angles only from that branch. Learn the table of domains and ranges, take care with the inverse of a trigonometric value, and draw each graph as a reflection in y equals x.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write the branch before the value
Negative inputs: the cosine family gives obtuse angles
For a domain, solve the double inequality
In graphs, mark end points and asymptotes

rows: the value inside the correct branch
reduce the angle, check the branch

visual.caption: ISC marks the method: show the branch you are using.

slides.narration: In the examination, always say which branch you are using before you give a value. Remember that the inverse cosine, cotangent and secant of a negative number give obtuse angles. For a domain, solve a double inequality. In a graph, mark the end points and any asymptotes.

decks.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions — Part 2: Properties, formulae and equations
goals: Use the rules for negative arguments and the complementary identities
Convert an inverse trigonometric expression from one function to another
Apply the sum and difference formulae for inverse tangent, sine and cosine with their conditions
Use the double and triple forms of the inverse tangent and inverse sine
Solve equations involving inverse trigonometric functions and test every root

slides.heading: Inverse Trigonometric Functions, Part 2
slides.body_md: Identities, formulae and equations: always with their conditions.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: negative arguments, complementary sums, converting between inverse functions, sum and difference formulae, double and triple forms, and solving equations.
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance.

slides.narration: In this part we work with inverse trigonometric functions algebraically. We start with simple properties, then combine two inverse tangents into one, use double and triple forms, and finally solve equations. Throughout, every formula comes with a condition, and checking that condition is where marks are won or lost.

slides.heading: Negative arguments
slides.body_md: $\sin^{-1}$, $\tan^{-1}$, $\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}$ are odd; $\cos^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cos^{-1} x$, and likewise for $\cot^{-1}$ and $\sec^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Table of the negative-argument rules, each checked numerically at x equals 0.6: inverse sine and inverse tangent are odd, while inverse cosine and inverse cotangent of minus x equal pi minus the value at x.
visual.caption: Odd for sine, tangent and cosecant; "pi minus" for cosine, cotangent and secant.

slides.narration: For the sine family and the tangent, a negative input simply gives a negative output. For the cosine family the answer must stay between zero and pi, so a negative input gives pi minus the value at the positive input. The table checks each rule at zero point six.

slides.heading: Complementary sums
slides.body_md: $\sin^{-1} x + \cos^{-1} x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $\tan^{-1} x + \cot^{-1} x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $\sec^{-1} x + \operatorname{cosec}^{-1} x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

visual.alt: Table of the three complementary identities with where each is valid and a numerical check: inverse sine plus inverse cosine, inverse tangent plus inverse cotangent, and inverse secant plus inverse cosecant all equal pi by 2.
visual.caption: Use these to change one inverse function into another.

slides.narration: Three pairs always add up to a right angle. If you know the inverse sine of a number, you know its inverse cosine too. These identities let you replace one inverse function by another, which is often the first step in solving an equation.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false?
slides.body_md: Is the inverse cosine an odd function?
slides.narration: Test it with minus one. The inverse cosine of minus one is pi.

slides.heading: One angle, many names
slides.body_md: For $0 < x \le 1$: $\cos^{-1} x = \sin^{-1}\sqrt{1 - x^2} = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}{x} = \sec^{-1}\dfrac1x$.

visual.alt: Table showing one angle written four ways for x equals 0.6: inverse cosine of 0.6, inverse sine of 0.8, inverse tangent of 4 by 3 and inverse secant of 5 by 3 all equal 0.9273 radians.
visual.caption: For $0 < x \le 1$: $\cos^{-1} x = \sin^{-1}\sqrt{1 - x^2} = \tan^{-1}\frac{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}{x}$.

slides.narration: Draw a right triangle with adjacent side x and hypotenuse one. The opposite side is the root of one minus x squared. Now the same acute angle can be named with any inverse function. At zero point six, all four names give the same angle, about zero point nine three radians.

slides.heading: Adding two inverse tangents
slides.body_md: $\tan^{-1} x + \tan^{-1} y = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{x + y}{1 - xy}$ when $xy < 1$; add or subtract $\pi$ when $xy > 1$.

visual.alt: Table of the inverse tangent addition formula in its three cases: product less than 1 gives the plain formula; product greater than 1 with both positive adds pi; with both negative subtracts pi; the difference formula needs the product greater than minus 1.
visual.caption: Always check the product before using the formula.

slides.narration: This is the most used formula of the chapter. When the product of the two numbers is less than one, the sum is the inverse tangent of x plus y over one minus x y. When the product is more than one, the sum leaves the principal range and we must add pi for positive numbers or subtract pi for negative ones.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a sum that is pi by four
slides.body_md: Show that $\tan^{-1}\dfrac34 + \tan^{-1}\dfrac17 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

visual.alt: Worked example table for inverse tangent of 3 by 4 plus inverse tangent of 1 by 7: the product 3 by 28 is less than 1, the formula gives 25 by 28 over 25 by 28, which is 1, so the sum is pi by 4.
visual.caption: Two awkward angles that add to exactly half a right angle.

slides.narration: First check the product: three quarters times one seventh is three over twenty eight, less than one. Then the formula applies. The numerator and denominator both work out to twenty five over twenty eight, so the fraction is one, and the inverse tangent of one is pi by four.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a difference
slides.body_md: Simplify $\tan^{-1}\dfrac12 - \tan^{-1}\dfrac13$.

visual.alt: Worked example table for inverse tangent of one half minus inverse tangent of one third: the product one sixth is greater than minus 1, the difference formula gives one sixth over seven sixths, so the answer is inverse tangent of one seventh.
visual.caption: Difference formula with its condition.

slides.narration: For a difference, the denominator becomes one plus x y, and the condition is that x y is greater than minus one. Here x y is one sixth. The fraction simplifies to one seventh, so the difference is the inverse tangent of one seventh.

slides.heading: Quick check: two angles of a set square
slides.body_md: Two inverse sines from a three, four, five triangle: what is their sum?
slides.narration: Draw the triangle. Is one angle the complement of the other?

slides.heading: Sums for inverse sine and cosine
slides.body_md: Name the angles $A$, $B$; expand $\sin(A \pm B)$ or $\cos(A + B)$; check the range.

visual.alt: Table of the sum and difference formulae for inverse sine and inverse cosine with the conditions under which they are used, which keep the combined angle inside the principal branch.
visual.caption: In practice, name the angles $A$ and $B$, expand $\sin(A \pm B)$ or $\cos(A + B)$, and check the range.

slides.narration: For inverse sines and cosines the formulas look heavy, but the method is simple. Call the two angles A and B, find their sines and cosines from right triangles, expand the sine or cosine of the sum, and finally check that the sum lies in the principal range of the function you want.

slides.heading: Double forms of the inverse tangent
slides.body_md: $2\tan^{-1} x = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{2x}{1 - x^2} = \sin^{-1}\dfrac{2x}{1 + x^2} = \cos^{-1}\dfrac{1 - x^2}{1 + x^2}$, each with its condition.

visual.alt: Table of three ways to write twice the inverse tangent of x: as an inverse tangent of 2 x over 1 minus x squared for x between minus 1 and 1, as an inverse sine of 2 x over 1 plus x squared for x between minus 1 and 1, and as an inverse cosine of 1 minus x squared over 1 plus x squared for non-negative x.
visual.caption: The conditions keep $2\tan^{-1} x$ inside each principal branch.

slides.narration: Twice an inverse tangent can be written three ways, using the double-angle formulas for tangent, sine and cosine. Each version needs its own condition, so that twice the angle stays inside the principal range of the outer function. Always write the condition next to the formula.

slides.heading: Where the double form is valid
slides.body_md: For $|x| < 1$ the curves $y = 2\tan^{-1} x$ and $y = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{2x}{1 - x^2}$ coincide.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals twice the inverse tangent of x, rising between minus pi and pi, drawn with the curve inverse tangent of 2 x over 1 minus x squared for x between minus 0.95 and 0.95. The two coincide on that interval, for example at the origin and at x equals 0.5.
visual.caption: For $|x| < 1$ the two curves are the same; outside it they differ by $\pm\pi$.

slides.narration: The graph shows twice the inverse tangent of x together with the inverse tangent of two x over one minus x squared. Between minus one and one they are the same curve. Outside that interval, twice the angle is beyond pi by two in size, and the two expressions differ by pi.

slides.heading: Quick check: a ramp angle
slides.body_md: Find the cosine of twice an inverse tangent.
slides.narration: Use the formula for cosine of a double angle in terms of the tangent.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: an equation with an extra root
slides.body_md: Solve $2\tan^{-1} x = \sin^{-1}\dfrac45$.
bullets: At $x = 2$, $2\tan^{-1} 2 > \frac{\pi}{2}$, which no inverse sine can equal: reject. Answer $x = \frac12$

visual.alt: Worked example table checking both roots of 2 x squared minus 5 x plus 2 equals 0 in twice the inverse tangent of x equals inverse sine of 4 by 5: at x equals one half both sides are 0.9273, so it is accepted; at x equals 2 the left side is 2.2143, so it is rejected.
visual.caption: Taking sines can add a root; test each one.

slides.narration: Taking the sine of both sides gives a quadratic with roots one half and two. Now test them. At two, twice the inverse tangent is more than pi by two, but an inverse sine is never more than pi by two, so two is rejected. Only one half satisfies the original equation.

slides.heading: Triple forms

visual.alt: Table of the triple forms with their conditions: three times the inverse tangent for x less than 1 over root 3 in size, three times the inverse sine for x at most one half in size, and three times the inverse cosine for x from one half to 1.
visual.caption: They come from $\tan 3\theta$, $\sin 3\theta$ and $\cos 3\theta$.

slides.narration: The triple forms come from the formulas for tangent, sine and cosine of three theta. The conditions are tighter than for the double forms, because three times the angle must stay inside the principal range. For the inverse tangent the input must be smaller than one over root three in size.

slides.heading: Quick check: the condition for the formula
slides.body_md: When is the inverse tangent addition formula guaranteed to hold?
slides.narration: Think about when the sum of the two angles stays between minus pi by two and pi by two.

slides.heading: Solving equations: a plan
slides.body_md: Combine, take a trigonometric function, solve, substitute back, reject.

nodes.label: Combine the inverse terms (sum, double or complementary formula)
Take tan, sin or cos of both sides
Substitute every root back into the original equation
Reject roots that break a condition or a range

visual.alt: Flow for solving equations with inverse trigonometric functions: combine the terms, take a trigonometric function of both sides, solve the algebra, substitute every root back, and reject roots that break a condition or a range.
visual.caption: The last two steps earn the final marks.

slides.narration: Here is a plan for every equation. Combine the inverse terms into one using a formula. Take the tangent, sine or cosine of both sides. Solve the algebra. Then substitute each root into the original equation. A root that breaks a condition, or makes the two sides different, must be rejected.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Negative inputs: odd, or pi minus
Sum formulae: check $xy < 1$ or the range
Double and triple forms need their conditions

nodes.label: Complementary pairs add to pi by 2

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 2: negative arguments make the function odd or give pi minus; complementary pairs add to pi by 2; sum formulae need their conditions; double and triple forms; and equations need every root checked.
visual.caption: Part 2 in one line.

slides.narration: To sum up. Negative inputs make the sine family odd and give pi minus for the cosine family. Complementary pairs add to a right angle. The sum formulae work only under their conditions, as do the double and triple forms. And when you solve an equation, every root must be tested in the original.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write the condition beside every formula
Never stop at the roots of the quadratic
Give exact answers in terms of $\pi$

rows: angles named 1, formula with condition 1, simplification 1
Value of a trigonometric function of an inverse (1–2)

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 2: an identity proof gives marks for naming the angles, using the formula with its condition and simplifying; an equation gives marks for combining, the algebra, testing and rejecting roots; double and triple forms need the condition checked; values of a trigonometric function of an inverse need the correct sign.
visual.caption: A condition that is never checked costs a mark.

slides.narration: Some final advice for the examination. Write the condition next to every formula you use. Name the angles before expanding a sine or cosine. Never stop at the roots of a quadratic: substitute them back and reject the ones that fail. And give answers exactly, in terms of pi, unless a decimal is asked for.

notes.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Principal-value branches
sections.body_md:
A trigonometric function is many-one, so it is first restricted to a **principal-value branch** on which it is one-one; the inverse returns angles only from that branch.

- $\sin^{-1}$: domain $[-1, 1]$, range $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$; $\cos^{-1}$: domain $[-1, 1]$, range $[0, \pi]$.
- $\tan^{-1}$: domain $\mathbb{R}$, range $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$; $\cot^{-1}$: domain $\mathbb{R}$, range $(0, \pi)$.
- $\sec^{-1}$: domain $\mathbb{R} - (-1, 1)$, range $[0, \pi] - \left\{\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right\}$; $\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}$: same domain, range $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] - \{0\}$.

$\sin^{-1} x$ is **not** $\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$.

key_terms.definition_md: The one value of an inverse trigonometric function that lies in its principal range.
The restricted interval on which a trigonometric function is one-one and is inverted.

visual.alt: Table of the six inverse trigonometric functions: sine and cosine inverses have domain minus 1 to 1, tangent and cotangent inverses have all reals, secant and cosecant inverses exclude the open interval minus 1 to 1; the principal ranges are listed beside each.
visual.caption: Learn this table: almost every principal-value question uses it.

visuals.alt: Worked example table of five principal values computed from the branches: inverse sine of minus one half is minus pi by 6, inverse cosine of root 3 by 2 is pi by 6, inverse tangent of minus 1 is minus pi by 4, inverse cotangent of minus 1 by root 3 is 2 pi by 3, inverse secant of root 2 is pi by 4.
visuals.caption: Each value is checked numerically when the chapter is built.

sections.heading: 2. Graphs
sections.body_md:
Each graph is the reflection of its branch in $y = x$.

- $\sin^{-1} x$ rises from $\left(-1, -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ through $(0, 0)$ to $\left(1, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ (odd).
- $\cos^{-1} x$ falls from $(-1, \pi)$ through $\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ to $(1, 0)$.
- $\tan^{-1} x$ rises between the asymptotes $y = \pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}$; $\cot^{-1} x$ falls between $y = \pi$ and $y = 0$.
- $\sec^{-1} x$ has two rising pieces and never reaches $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

Transformations scale and shift the range: $y = 3\cos^{-1} x - \pi$ lies in $[-\pi, 2\pi]$.

key_terms.definition_md: A line such as $y = \frac{\pi}{2}$ that the graph of $\tan^{-1} x$ approaches but never meets.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals the inverse sine of x for x from minus 1 to 1: it rises from the point minus 1, minus pi by 2 through the origin to the point 1, pi by 2, steepest at the two ends.
visual.caption: Domain $[-1, 1]$, range $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$; an odd, increasing function.

visuals.alt: Graph of y equals the inverse cosine of x: it falls from the point minus 1, pi through the point 0, pi by 2 to the point 1, 0 on the x-axis. It is a decreasing curve lying between heights 0 and pi.
visuals.caption: Domain $[-1, 1]$, range $[0, \pi]$; a decreasing function.

visuals.alt: Graphs of the inverse tangent, rising between the horizontal asymptotes minus pi by 2 and pi by 2, and of the inverse cotangent, falling between pi and 0. They cross at the point 1, pi by 4, and the cotangent curve passes 0, pi by 2.
visuals.caption: The two curves add up to $\frac{\pi}{2}$ at every $x$.

visuals.alt: Table of four angles, their sines and the inverse sine of each sine: only pi by 3 comes back unchanged; 5 pi by 6 returns pi by 6, 7 pi by 6 returns minus pi by 6, and minus 3 pi by 4 returns minus pi by 4.
visuals.caption: The inverse sine always answers inside $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$.

sections.heading: 3. Elementary properties
sections.body_md:
- **Negative arguments:** $\sin^{-1}(-x) = -\sin^{-1} x$, $\tan^{-1}(-x) = -\tan^{-1} x$, $\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(-x) = -\operatorname{cosec}^{-1} x$; $\cos^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cos^{-1} x$, $\cot^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cot^{-1} x$, $\sec^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \sec^{-1} x$.
- **Reciprocal relations:** $\sin^{-1}\dfrac1x = \operatorname{cosec}^{-1} x$ and $\cos^{-1}\dfrac1x = \sec^{-1} x$ for $|x| \ge 1$; $\tan^{-1}\dfrac1x = \cot^{-1} x$ for $x > 0$ and $\cot^{-1} x - \pi$ for $x < 0$.
- **Complementary sums:** $\sin^{-1} x + \cos^{-1} x = \tan^{-1} x + \cot^{-1} x = \sec^{-1} x + \operatorname{cosec}^{-1} x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
- **Interconversion:** draw the right triangle; for example $\sin^{-1} x = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}$ for $|x| < 1$.

sections.heading: 4. Sum and difference formulae
sections.body_md:
- $\tan^{-1} x + \tan^{-1} y = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{x + y}{1 - xy}$ if $xy < 1$; $= \pi + \tan^{-1}\dfrac{x + y}{1 - xy}$ if $xy > 1$, $x, y > 0$; $= -\pi + \tan^{-1}\dfrac{x + y}{1 - xy}$ if $xy > 1$, $x, y < 0$.
- $\tan^{-1} x - \tan^{-1} y = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{x - y}{1 + xy}$ if $xy > -1$.
- For $\sin^{-1}$ and $\cos^{-1}$: name the angles $A$ and $B$, expand $\sin(A \pm B)$ or $\cos(A \pm B)$ from right triangles, and check that the result lies in the principal range.

sections.heading: 6. Solving equations
sections.body_md:
1. Combine the inverse terms with a sum, double or complementary formula.
2. Take $\tan$, $\sin$ or $\cos$ of both sides.
3. Solve the algebraic equation.
4. Substitute **every** root into the original equation; reject roots that break a condition or give a value outside a principal range.

Example: $2\tan^{-1} x = \sin^{-1}\dfrac45$ gives $2x^2 - 5x + 2 = 0$, roots $\dfrac12$ and $2$; only $\dfrac12$ survives.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How ISC marks are awarded**
- *Principal value (1 mark):* only a value in the correct branch earns the mark.
- *Identity proofs (3 marks):* angles named, formula with its condition, simplification.
- *Equations (3–5 marks):* combining, algebra, testing each root and rejecting with a reason.
- *Section D (5 marks):* questions come in parts such as 2 + 3; label each part.

**Common mistakes**
- Reading $\sin^{-1} x$ as $\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$.
- Cancelling $\sin^{-1}(\sin\theta)$ to $\theta$ when $\theta$ is outside the branch.
- Using the inverse tangent addition formula when $xy > 1$.
- Giving a negative value for $\cos^{-1}$, $\cot^{-1}$ or $\sec^{-1}$.
- Keeping both roots of the quadratic without checking them.

cards.front_md: Why must $\sin x$ be restricted before inverting it?
cards.back_md: It is many-one on $\mathbb{R}$; on $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ it is one-one and onto $[-1, 1]$.

cards.front_md: Is $\sin^{-1} x$ the same as $\frac{1}{\sin x}$?
cards.back_md: No: it is the angle whose sine is $x$.

cards.front_md: How to get the graph of $\sin^{-1} x$

cards.back_md: Name the angles, expand $\sin(A + B)$, check the range.

cards.front_md: Last step in solving any inverse-trigonometric equation
cards.back_md: Substitute every root back and reject those that fail.

questions.stem_md: Which interval contains every principal value produced by the inverse tangent function?
questions.solution_md: $\tan^{-1} x$ takes every value strictly between $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, but never the end points, because $\tan$ is undefined there. $[0, \pi]$ is the range for $\cos^{-1}$ and $(0, \pi)$ for $\cot^{-1}$.

questions.stem_md: A calculator in radian mode is asked for $\cos^{-1}(-0.5)$. Written in terms of $\pi$, the value it displays is
questions.solution_md: The principal value lies in $[0, \pi]$. Since $\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac12$, the angle with cosine $-\dfrac12$ in that interval is $\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

questions.stem_md: A crank designer needs the principal value of $\sin^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$ to set a starting angle. Which value should be used?
questions.solution_md: $\sin^{-1}$ returns angles in $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$, and $\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$. The other angles have the right sine but lie outside the principal branch.

questions.stem_md: Using the principal branch $(0, \pi)$ for the inverse cotangent, the value of $\cot^{-1}(-\sqrt{3})$ is
questions.solution_md: $\cot\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \sqrt3$, so in $(0, \pi)$ the angle with cotangent $-\sqrt3$ is $\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$. The value $-\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ lies outside $(0, \pi)$.

questions.stem_md: A surveyor's table gives $\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\right)$. Its principal value is
questions.solution_md: $\operatorname{cosec}\theta = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}$ means $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$. In $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] - \{0\}$ this gives $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

questions.stem_md: For which set of real numbers is the inverse secant function $\sec^{-1} x$ defined?
questions.solution_md: $|\sec\theta| \ge 1$ whenever it is defined, so $\sec^{-1} x$ needs $x \le -1$ or $x \ge 1$, that is $\mathbb{R} - (-1, 1)$.

questions.stem_md: A spreadsheet formula uses $\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x - 4}{3}\right)$. For which values of $x$ does the formula give a real answer?
questions.solution_md: We need $-1 \le \dfrac{x - 4}{3} \le 1$, i.e. $-3 \le x - 4 \le 3$, i.e. $1 \le x \le 7$.

questions.stem_md: An angle of $\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$ is fed into $\sin$ and the result straight into $\sin^{-1}$. Which angle comes out?
questions.solution_md: $\sin\dfrac{7\pi}{6} = -\dfrac12$, and the principal value of $\sin^{-1}\left(-\dfrac12\right)$ is $-\dfrac{\pi}{6}$. $\sin^{-1}(\sin\theta) = \theta$ only for $\theta$ in $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$.

questions.stem_md: What does $\cos^{-1}\left(\cos\left(-\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\right)\right)$ simplify to, given that cosine is an even function?
questions.solution_md: $\cos\left(-\dfrac{2\pi}{5}\right) = \cos\dfrac{2\pi}{5}$ and $\dfrac{2\pi}{5}$ lies in $[0, \pi]$, so the value is $\dfrac{2\pi}{5}$.

questions.stem_md: Applying $\tan^{-1}$ to $\tan\dfrac{4\pi}{5}$ returns an angle in the principal branch. Which one?
questions.solution_md: $\tan$ has period $\pi$: $\tan\dfrac{4\pi}{5} = \tan\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{5} - \pi\right) = \tan\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{5}\right)$, and $-\dfrac{\pi}{5}$ lies in $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

questions.stem_md: A student plots the curve $y = \cos^{-1} x$ on graph paper. Which of these points should lie on the curve?
questions.solution_md: $\cos^{-1} 0 = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$. The curve starts at $(-1, \pi)$, passes $\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ and ends at $(1, 0)$; the other points are not on it.

questions.stem_md: Among the following inverse functions, which one falls steadily (is decreasing) on its whole domain?
questions.solution_md: $\cos^{-1} x$ falls from $\pi$ at $x = -1$ to $0$ at $x = 1$. $\sin^{-1} x$ and $\tan^{-1} x$ rise throughout, and $\sec^{-1} x$ rises on each of its two pieces.

questions.stem_md: The curve $y = 3\cos^{-1} x - \pi$ is drawn for $-1 \le x \le 1$. Between which heights does it lie?
questions.solution_md: $0 \le \cos^{-1} x \le \pi$, so $0 \le 3\cos^{-1} x \le 3\pi$ and $-\pi \le 3\cos^{-1} x - \pi \le 2\pi$.

questions.stem_md: The graph of $y = \sin^{-1} x$ is obtained by reflecting, in the line $y = x$, the graph of $y = \sin x$ restricted to
questions.solution_md: On $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ the sine function is one-one and takes every value in $[-1, 1]$; its reflection in $y = x$ is the principal branch of $\sin^{-1} x$.

questions.stem_md: Without using a calculator, a student adds $\sin^{-1}(0.3)$ and $\cos^{-1}(0.3)$. The total is
questions.solution_md: For every $x$ in $[-1, 1]$, $\sin^{-1} x + \cos^{-1} x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$; the value $0.3$ does not matter.

questions.stem_md: If $\cos^{-1}(0.2) = \alpha$, then the inverse cosine of the negative number $-0.2$ equals
questions.solution_md: $\cos^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cos^{-1} x$ for $x$ in $[-1, 1]$, so the value is $\pi - \alpha$. Note that $-\alpha$ would be negative, outside $[0, \pi]$.

questions.stem_md: For a negative real number $x$, the reciprocal relation between inverse tangent and inverse cotangent says that $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{x}$ equals
questions.solution_md: For $x < 0$, $\cot^{-1} x$ lies in $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right)$ while $\tan^{-1}\dfrac1x$ lies in $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right)$; both have cotangent $x$, and they differ by $\pi$. So $\tan^{-1}\dfrac1x = \cot^{-1} x - \pi$. (For $x > 0$ the two are equal.)

questions.stem_md: For $-1 < x < 1$, which inverse tangent expression is identical to $\sin^{-1} x$?
questions.solution_md: Put $\sin^{-1} x = \theta$ in $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$; then $\cos\theta = \sqrt{1 - x^2} > 0$ and $\tan\theta = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}$, so $\theta = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}$.

questions.stem_md: A right triangle has hypotenuse $5$ and adjacent side $3$, so one acute angle is $\sec^{-1}\dfrac{5}{3}$. The same angle can be written as
questions.solution_md: $\sec\theta = \dfrac53$ gives $\cos\theta = \dfrac35$, opposite side $4$, so $\tan\theta = \dfrac43$ and $\theta = \tan^{-1}\dfrac43$. The other three are the complementary angle.

questions.stem_md: Using the addition formula for inverse tangents (the product of the two numbers is less than $1$), $\tan^{-1}\dfrac14 + \tan^{-1}\dfrac35$ simplifies to
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{\frac14 + \frac35}{1 - \frac14 \cdot \frac35} = \dfrac{\frac{17}{20}}{\frac{17}{20}} = 1$, and $xy = \dfrac{3}{20} < 1$, so the sum is $\tan^{-1} 1 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

questions.stem_md: Two positive numbers $2$ and $3$ have product greater than $1$. The sum $\tan^{-1} 2 + \tan^{-1} 3$ equals
questions.solution_md: Here $xy = 6 > 1$ with $x, y > 0$, so the sum is $\pi + \tan^{-1}\dfrac{2 + 3}{1 - 6} = \pi + \tan^{-1}(-1) = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$. Each term lies in $\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, so the sum must be positive.

questions.stem_md: Under which condition on the real numbers $x$ and $y$ is $\tan^{-1} x + \tan^{-1} y = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{x + y}{1 - xy}$ guaranteed?
questions.solution_md: When $xy < 1$ the sum of the two principal values stays inside $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, so it equals the principal value on the right. For $xy > 1$ a correction of $\pm \pi$ is needed.

questions.stem_md: In a right-angled set square the two acute angles are $\sin^{-1}\dfrac35$ and $\sin^{-1}\dfrac45$. Their sum is
questions.solution_md: $\sin^{-1}\dfrac45 = \cos^{-1}\dfrac35$ (sides $3, 4, 5$), so the sum is $\sin^{-1}\dfrac35 + \cos^{-1}\dfrac35 = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

questions.stem_md: Using the difference formula for inverse cosines, $\cos^{-1}\dfrac45 - \cos^{-1}\dfrac{12}{13}$ can be written as
questions.solution_md: With $\cos A = \dfrac45$, $\sin A = \dfrac35$, $\cos B = \dfrac{12}{13}$, $\sin B = \dfrac{5}{13}$: $\cos(A - B) = \dfrac{48}{65} + \dfrac{15}{65} = \dfrac{63}{65}$. Since $A > B$, $A - B$ lies in $[0, \pi]$, so it equals $\cos^{-1}\dfrac{63}{65}$.

questions.stem_md: Using the double-angle form of the inverse tangent, $2\tan^{-1}\dfrac13$ equals
questions.solution_md: $2\tan^{-1} x = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{2x}{1 - x^2}$ for $|x| < 1$: $\dfrac{\frac23}{1 - \frac19} = \dfrac{\frac23}{\frac89} = \dfrac34$.

questions.stem_md: For $|x| < \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$, the triple-angle form gives $3\tan^{-1} x$ as
questions.solution_md: With $\theta = \tan^{-1} x$, $\tan 3\theta = \dfrac{3\tan\theta - \tan^3\theta}{1 - 3\tan^2\theta}$; for $|x| < \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$, $3\theta$ stays in $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

questions.stem_md: For which values of $x$ is $2\sin^{-1} x = \sin^{-1}\left(2x\sqrt{1 - x^2}\right)$ true?
questions.solution_md: $2\sin^{-1} x$ must itself lie in $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$, so $\sin^{-1} x$ lies in $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]$, i.e. $|x| \le \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$.

questions.stem_md: A student solves $\tan^{-1}(2x) + \tan^{-1}(3x) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and obtains the quadratic $6x^2 + 5x - 1 = 0$. Which value(s) of $x$ actually satisfy the original equation?
questions.solution_md: The roots are $\dfrac16$ and $-1$. At $x = -1$ both angles are negative, so their sum is negative and cannot be $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. At $x = \dfrac16$: $\tan^{-1}\dfrac13 + \tan^{-1}\dfrac12 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. A is true because $\tan$ is increasing on $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, so its inverse is increasing; being defined everywhere (R) does not explain this.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The inverse sine is an odd function: $\sin^{-1}(-x) = -\sin^{-1} x$ for every $x$ in $[-1, 1]$.
questions.solution_md: True: both sides lie in $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ and have sine $-x$.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Just like the inverse sine, the inverse cosine satisfies $\cos^{-1}(-x) = -\cos^{-1} x$.
questions.solution_md: False: $\cos^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cos^{-1} x$. For example $\cos^{-1}(-1) = \pi$, not $-0$.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Combining a tangent value with a secant value, $\tan^{-1}\sqrt3 - \sec^{-1}(-2) = -\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
questions.solution_md: True: $\tan^{-1}\sqrt3 = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $\sec^{-1}(-2) = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$, so the difference is $-\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The equation $\sin^{-1} x = 2$ has a real solution, because $\sin^{-1}$ is defined on all of $[-1, 1]$.
questions.solution_md: False: $\sin^{-1} x$ never exceeds $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.57$, so it cannot equal $2$.

questions.stem_md: The principal value of the inverse secant at $-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}$, written as a multiple of $\pi$, is ___.
questions.solution_md: $\sec\theta = -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}$ means $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$; in $[0, \pi]$, $\theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$, written 5π/6.

questions.stem_md: If $\tan^{-1} x = \dfrac{\pi}{10}$ for a positive $x$, then the inverse cotangent of the same $x$ is ___ (as a multiple of $\pi$).
questions.solution_md: $\tan^{-1} x + \cot^{-1} x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so $\cot^{-1} x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{10} = \dfrac{2\pi}{5}$, written 2π/5.

questions.stem_md: Adding the inverse cosine of one half to twice the inverse sine of one half gives ___ (as a multiple of $\pi$).
questions.solution_md: $\cos^{-1}\dfrac12 + 2\sin^{-1}\dfrac12 = \dfrac{\pi}{3} + \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$, written 2π/3.

questions.stem_md: Give, in degrees, the principal value of the inverse cosecant at $-2$.
questions.solution_md: $\operatorname{cosec}\theta = -2$ means $\sin\theta = -\dfrac12$; in $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] - \{0\}$, $\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{6} = -30°$.

questions.stem_md: Evaluate $\tan\left(\tan^{-1} 4 - \tan^{-1}\dfrac35\right)$.
questions.solution_md: $\tan(A - B) = \dfrac{4 - \frac35}{1 + 4 \cdot \frac35} = \dfrac{\frac{17}{5}}{\frac{17}{5}} = 1$.

questions.stem_md: A ramp makes the angle $2\tan^{-1}\dfrac17$ with the floor. Find the cosine of this angle as a decimal.
questions.solution_md: $\cos 2\theta = \dfrac{1 - \tan^2\theta}{1 + \tan^2\theta} = \dfrac{1 - \frac{1}{49}}{1 + \frac{1}{49}} = \dfrac{48}{50} = 0.96$.

questions.stem_md: Find the real number $x$ for which the inverse cosine of $x$ is exactly twice its inverse sine, $\cos^{-1} x = 2\sin^{-1} x$.
questions.solution_md: Write $\sin^{-1} x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \cos^{-1} x$: then $\cos^{-1} x = \pi - 2\cos^{-1} x$, so $\cos^{-1} x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $x = 0.5$.

questions.stem_md: Find the value of $\tan\left(\dfrac12\cos^{-1}\dfrac35\right)$.
questions.solution_md: With $\cos 2\phi = \dfrac35$ and $\phi$ acute, $\tan\phi = \sqrt{\dfrac{1 - \frac35}{1 + \frac35}} = \sqrt{\dfrac14} = 0.5$.

questions.stem_md: Find the value of $\cos\left(2\sin^{-1} 0.6\right)$.
Evaluate $\sin^{-1}\left(-\dfrac12\right) + \cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac12\right)$ using principal values, and name the identity your answer agrees with.

**(b)** $\tan^{-1}\dfrac79 + \tan^{-1}\dfrac18$: product $\dfrac{7}{72} < 1$, so the sum is $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{\frac79 + \frac18}{1 - \frac{7}{72}} = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{\frac{65}{72}}{\frac{65}{72}} = \tan^{-1} 1 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

questions.stem_md:
Consider the equation $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{x}{2} + \tan^{-1}\dfrac{x}{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

(a) Take tangents of both sides and obtain the possible values of $x$. [3]

(b) Decide which value(s) satisfy the original equation, giving a reason for any rejection. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\dfrac{\frac{x}{2} + \frac{x}{3}}{1 - \frac{x^2}{6}} = 1 \Rightarrow \dfrac{5x}{6} = 1 - \dfrac{x^2}{6} \Rightarrow x^2 + 5x - 6 = 0 \Rightarrow (x + 6)(x - 1) = 0$, so $x = 1$ or $x = -6$.

**(b)** $x = 1$: $\tan^{-1}\dfrac12 + \tan^{-1}\dfrac13$, product $\dfrac16 < 1$, gives $\tan^{-1} 1 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$. ✓

$x = -6$: $\tan^{-1}(-3) + \tan^{-1}(-2)$; both angles are negative (and the product $6 > 1$), so the sum is $-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$, not $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$: reject. The solution is $x = 1$.
